paper.title: Time to retire? A register-based study of GPs’ practice style prior to retirement
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement is given. On data access the paper states: …

registers.role: treatment (date of retirement), sample frame (single-handed vs partnership practice), linkage
variables_mentioned: whether the GP is in a partnership or a single-handed practice

registers.role: outcomes (provided services, obtained fees, referrals to private practice specialists)
variables_mentioned: referrals made to private practice specialists

registers.role: controls (patients' and GPs' ICD-10 codes at hospitals, used to calculate the Charlson Comorbidity Index)
outcome (costs of all patient-purchased prescription drugs per year)
variables_mentioned: patients' purchase of prescription drugs at pharmacies

registers.role: controls (GPs' and patients' socioeconomic information; average equivalent disposable family income)

variables_mentioned: proportion of patients with primary/preparatory education
proportion of patients who are retired

linkages: GPs are identified by their social security number being linked to a provider number in the provider register.
Patients are linked to the general practice they are enlisted with, which gives practice-level list size, patient flows and patient characteristics.
GPs' and their patients' socioeconomic information is linked from Statistics Denmark's IND, FAIK, FAM, BEF and DREAM registers.
Patients' and GPs' hospital ICD-10 codes from the National Patient Register are used to compute Charlson Comorbidity Indices.

sample.universe: Danish general practitioners and their enlisted patients aged 18 and above; in 2017 there were 3436 GPs in Denmark.
sample.unit_of_observation: single-handed general practice (GP) x calendar year
selection_rules: (i) only single-handed GPs, because services cannot be attributed to an individual GP in partnership practices
(ii) GPs excluded if they change practice or are affiliated to multiple practices during the analysis period (to ensure a balanced panel)
(iii) GPs must be active throughout the analysis period, defined as billing at least one service per year continuously
(iv) practices excluded if they have had multiple owners in at least one year of the analysis period
(v) only GPs who retire above the age of 60 are included, to minimise 'acute' retirement decisions
(vi) GPs excluded if they have fewer than 500 patients on their lists
(vii) GPs must have a social security number registered in the provider register, to allow linkage to other registers
Retiring GPs are those who retire within 2015-2017; non-retiring GPs are those who have not retired by the end of 2017
Each retiring GP is observed for the ten years up to retirement; the year of retirement itself is dropped
sample.period: 2005-2016 for the estimation sample (data 2005 to 2017; GPs retiring in 2015 are observed 2005-2014, GPs retiring in 2017 are observed 2007-2016)
sample.n_observations: 6,346 GP-years (5,885 for the outcome 'number of patients joining the list')
sample.n_individuals: 555 single-handed practices: 398 non-retiring GPs and 157 retiring GPs

construction_notes: All practice style outcomes enter in natural logs, so estimates are percentage differences; the paper states all coefficients can be interpreted as %Δy = 100·(e^β - 1).
Balanced panel of GPs over a ten-year observation period; the choice of a balanced sample is said to ensure stability in the practice style outcomes.
Models are augmented with Mundlak correction terms: GP-level means of all time-varying covariates except the yearfrom dummies and the calendar-year dummies.
List size is controlled for in all outcomes except list size, join and leave, so that estimates are interpreted 'per enlisted patient'.
The patient population (and list size) includes only patients aged 18 years and above.
Patients leaving the list are counted only when they leave without changing residence, which indicates an active choice of changing GP.
The number of referrals to private practising specialists is quantified using the separate fee these specialists receive for a consultation related to a new referral.
The Charlson Comorbidity Index is computed from ICD-10 codes in the National Patient Register, 1996-2016.
GP wealth is proxied by average equivalent disposable family income (DKK) from 1996 to 2004.
Standard errors are clustered at GP level.
Descriptive statistics in Table 1 are averages at practice level across 2005 to 2016.

claims.statement: Conditional on GP age, patient characteristics, geography and calendar year, the number of patients on their list (in logs) of single-handed Danish GPs observed 10 years before retirement does not differ statistically from that of GPs who are not retiring during the analysis period.

treatment.label: Being 10 years from retirement (10.yearfrom), i.e. a retiring GP observed 10 years before retirement, relative to GPs who are not retiring during the analysis period

register_source.value: Provider register (GPs' date of retirement; a GP is defined as retired when they no longer appear in the provider register; GPs are identified by their social security number being linked to a provider number)

definition.value: Dummy variable in the vector yearfrom indicating that the retiring GP is 10 years from retirement. The vector covers year 10 to year 1 before retirement; the GP's year of retirement itself is disregarded because the exact retirement date is uncertain. Retiring GPs are those who retire within 2015-2017; the reference category is GPs who are not retiring during the analysis period (not retired by the end of 2017).

timing.value: Calendar year t that falls 10 years before the GP's retirement year (within 2005-2016); the retirement year itself is excluded.

definition.value: Natural log of the number of patients enlisted on the GP's list in a given year. The patient population (and list size) includes only patients aged 18 years and above. Measured at single-handed-practice level per calendar year; list size is not controlled for when it is itself the outcome.

timing.value: Measured in the same calendar year t as the treatment dummy, i.e. 10 years before retirement; annual totals at practice level.

units.value: log points (coefficient on the natural log of the outcome); the paper states all estimates can be interpreted as %Δy = 100·(e^β - 1)

estimand.target_population: Single-handed Danish general practices (GPs) observed in a balanced ten-year panel within 2005-2016; the contrast is between GPs who retire within 2015-2017 and GPs who have not retired by the end of 2017.

population.description: 555 single-handed Danish general practices (398 non-retiring GPs and 157 retiring GPs) and their enlisted patients aged 18 and above, observed as a balanced panel over a ten-year period within 2005-2016.
population.ages: Retiring GPs are 57.13 years old on average at baseline and non-retiring GPs 50.71; GPs who retire below the age of 60 are excluded. Patients are aged 18 and above.
subgroups_defined: retiring GPs vs non-retiring GPs
early retirees (retiring before the state pension age of 65) vs late retirees (retiring at 65 or above)
population.selection: Seven exclusion criteria: single-handed practices only; GPs excluded if they change practice or are affiliated to multiple practices during the analysis period; GPs must be active (billing at least one service per year) throughout the period; practices with multiple owners in any year excluded; only GPs retiring above age 60 included; GPs with fewer than 500 patients on their lists excluded; GPs must have a social security number registered in the provider register. The panel is balanced over ten years.

identification.source_of_variation: Observational contrast between single-handed GPs who retire within 2015-2017, indexed by dummies for the number of years before retirement, and GPs who have not retired by the end of 2017, conditional on GP age (cohort), patient population characteristics, geography, calendar year, list size and Mundlak GP-level means. No reform, lottery or discontinuity is used; the authors describe the estimate as an association.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the GP's age, their patients' characteristics, geographical area, list size, calendar year and the Mundlak GP-level means of the time-varying covariates, being a given number of years from retirement is unrelated to the remaining (unobserved) determinants of practice style, so the estimated difference is the 'retirement effect' over and above a cohort effect and exogenous factors.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper motivates each control (age for cohort, patient characteristics for demand, calendar year for time trends, geography for access to secondary care) and adds Mundlak correction terms to absorb time-invariant GP and patient characteristics; it does not test the assumption and frames results as associations.

given: Mundlak GP-level means of time-varying covariates

key_assumptions.assumption: The cohort effect is separated from the 'retirement effect' by the control for the GP's own age; the authors concede this separation may be imperfect, especially for the late retirees, because few non-retiring GPs are as old as the late retirees.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test; the paper states in the discussion that it cannot exclude the possibility that a cohort effect is imperfectly separated from the 'retirement effect' and thereby (partly) drives the results.

implies_edges.from: cohort effect (GP birth cohort not captured by age)

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditioning the sample on being a single-handed practice that is active (billing at least one service per year), has at least 500 enlisted patients, has a single owner and is observed in a balanced ten-year panel does not distort the comparison.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper motivates the balanced sample as ensuring stability of practice style outcomes and reports a supplementary analysis with a five-year period (appendix A4), in which all results except 'the number of patients joining the list per year' are robust.

implies_edges.to: sample inclusion (active single-handed practice with >=500 patients, balanced ten-year panel)

key_assumptions.assumption: A GP's retirement is correctly dated by their disappearance from the provider register; because the exact retirement date is uncertain the year of retirement itself is dropped, and GPs who continue consulting after selling their provider number (e.g. as a locum) are treated as retired.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in section 4; no validation is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The log-linear specification is correct: the 'retirement effect' enters as an additive shift in the log outcome that is constant across GPs within a given year-from-retirement and additively separable from the controls.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Implied by equation (1); the paper justifies the log transformation as making estimates interpretable as percentage differences and as alleviating right-skewness, but does not test the functional form.

formal.as_written: ln(yit) = β1yearfromit + β2ageit + β3patit + β4geoi + β5listsizeit + Tt + εit,

threats_discussed: A cohort effect may be imperfectly separated from the 'retirement effect', especially for late retirees, because few non-retiring GPs are of the same old age.
Non-retiring GPs are on average only 6.4 years younger and a significant share of them may also be nearing retirement, which makes the estimate conservative.
The analysis covers only single-handed practices, who may behave differently from GPs in partnership practices; estimates are likely conservative relative to partnership practices.
The goodwill/selling-price rule gives GPs a financial incentive to maintain revenue in the last three years, which would make the estimates conservative; the authors argue the incentive is weak.
The Charlson Comorbidity Index is an imperfect proxy for GPs' and patients' health status.
The outcome set is limited by register content and cannot capture all clinically relevant behaviour or the quality of care.
The balanced ten-year sample is restrictive and may select GPs.
robustness_checks: Model 2: the same specification augmented with observable GP characteristics (gender, number of children, marital status, previously generated income, health status) - appendix A3.
Heterogeneity analysis splitting retiring GPs by whether they retire before or after the state pension age of 65.
Reducing the analysis period from ten to five years (appendix A4); all results are robust except 'the number of patients joining the list per year'.
Estimating the models without the time-averaged (Mundlak) covariates using OLS with standard errors clustered at GP level (appendix A6).
unresolved_confounders: A cohort effect that is imperfectly separated from the 'retirement effect', which the authors say they cannot exclude as (partly) driving the results, in particular for the late retirees.

ambiguities: The paper describes every estimate as an association (a 'retirement effect' defined as the association between practice style and years from retirement over and above a cohort effect), not as a causal effect; identification.strategy is recorded as selection_on_observables because the design rests on adjusting for observed cohort, patient, geographic and time factors, but 'descriptive' would also be defensible.

baseline_mean and outcome_sd are the non-retiring GPs' mean and standard deviation of the outcome in levels (Table 1, averages at practice level over 2005-2016); the regression outcome is the natural log of that variable, so the two are not in identical units. The paper itself uses the Table 1 non-retiring mean this way when interpreting the home-visit estimates.
The coefficient carries no significance star, so sign is recorded as 'null'; the point estimate itself is negative (-0.014).

evidence.how: The coefficient carries no significance star and Table 2's note defines *p < 0.10, **p < 0.05, ***p < 0.01; the estimate is therefore not statistically distinguishable from zero at the 10% level, which is how the paper reads the absence of a 'retirement effect'.

value.parameter_of_interest: β1 (the vector of coefficients on the yearfrom dummies)
value.normalisation: Reference category for the yearfrom dummies is GPs who are not retiring during the analysis period; calendar-year dummies have baseline 2005; region dummies have baseline The North Denmark Region; the urban indicator has baseline rural; the outcome is in natural logs; listsizeit is omitted when the outcome is list size, join or leave.

value.claimed_domain: Danish single-handed general practice, where GPs are remunerated primarily through fee-for-service and work under contract with the Danish Regions.
boundary_conditions: Policymakers should be careful generalising the findings to settings where GPs' market conditions are markedly different than in Denmark.
The results may not hold when GPs are paid by other payment schemes than fee-for-service.
GPs in partnership practices may behave differently from the single-handed GPs studied; for them the estimated 'retirement effect' would likely be larger (the estimates here are conservative).

register_source.value: Provider register (GPs' date of retirement; a GP is defined as retired when they no longer appear in the provider register; GPs are identified by their social security number being linked to a provider number)

definition.value: Dummy variable in the vector yearfrom indicating that the retiring GP is 3 years from retirement. The vector covers year 10 to year 1 before retirement; the GP's year of retirement itself is disregarded because the exact retirement date is uncertain. Retiring GPs are those who retire within 2015-2017; the reference category is GPs who are not retiring during the analysis period (not retired by the end of 2017).

timing.value: Calendar year t that falls 3 years before the GP's retirement year (within 2005-2016); the retirement year itself is excluded.

definition.value: Natural log of the number of patients leaving the GP's list in a given year. The paper focuses on patients leaving the GP without changing residence, because this indicates an active choice of changing the GP. List size is not controlled for for this outcome.

timing.value: Measured in the same calendar year t as the treatment dummy, i.e. 3 years before retirement; annual totals at practice level.

units.value: log points (coefficient on the natural log of the outcome); the paper states all estimates can be interpreted as %Δy = 100·(e^β - 1)

estimand.target_population: Single-handed Danish general practices (GPs) observed in a balanced ten-year panel within 2005-2016; the contrast is between GPs who retire within 2015-2017 and GPs who have not retired by the end of 2017.

population.description: 555 single-handed Danish general practices (398 non-retiring GPs and 157 retiring GPs) and their enlisted patients aged 18 and above, observed as a balanced panel over a ten-year period within 2005-2016.
population.ages: Retiring GPs are 57.13 years old on average at baseline and non-retiring GPs 50.71; GPs who retire below the age of 60 are excluded. Patients are aged 18 and above.
subgroups_defined: retiring GPs vs non-retiring GPs
early retirees (retiring before the state pension age of 65) vs late retirees (retiring at 65 or above)
population.selection: Seven exclusion criteria: single-handed practices only; GPs excluded if they change practice or are affiliated to multiple practices during the analysis period; GPs must be active (billing at least one service per year) throughout the period; practices with multiple owners in any year excluded; only GPs retiring above age 60 included; GPs with fewer than 500 patients on their lists excluded; GPs must have a social security number registered in the provider register. The panel is balanced over ten years.

identification.source_of_variation: Observational contrast between single-handed GPs who retire within 2015-2017, indexed by dummies for the number of years before retirement, and GPs who have not retired by the end of 2017, conditional on GP age (cohort), patient population characteristics, geography, calendar year, list size and Mundlak GP-level means. No reform, lottery or discontinuity is used; the authors describe the estimate as an association.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the GP's age, their patients' characteristics, geographical area, list size, calendar year and the Mundlak GP-level means of the time-varying covariates, being a given number of years from retirement is unrelated to the remaining (unobserved) determinants of practice style, so the estimated difference is the 'retirement effect' over and above a cohort effect and exogenous factors.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper motivates each control (age for cohort, patient characteristics for demand, calendar year for time trends, geography for access to secondary care) and adds Mundlak correction terms to absorb time-invariant GP and patient characteristics; it does not test the assumption and frames results as associations.

given: Mundlak GP-level means of time-varying covariates

key_assumptions.assumption: The cohort effect is separated from the 'retirement effect' by the control for the GP's own age; the authors concede this separation may be imperfect, especially for the late retirees, because few non-retiring GPs are as old as the late retirees.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test; the paper states in the discussion that it cannot exclude the possibility that a cohort effect is imperfectly separated from the 'retirement effect' and thereby (partly) drives the results.

implies_edges.from: cohort effect (GP birth cohort not captured by age)
cohort effect (GP birth cohort not captured by age)

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditioning the sample on being a single-handed practice that is active (billing at least one service per year), has at least 500 enlisted patients, has a single owner and is observed in a balanced ten-year panel does not distort the comparison.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper motivates the balanced sample as ensuring stability of practice style outcomes and reports a supplementary analysis with a five-year period (appendix A4), in which all results except 'the number of patients joining the list per year' are robust.

implies_edges.to: sample inclusion (active single-handed practice with >=500 patients, balanced ten-year panel)

key_assumptions.assumption: A GP's retirement is correctly dated by their disappearance from the provider register; because the exact retirement date is uncertain the year of retirement itself is dropped, and GPs who continue consulting after selling their provider number (e.g. as a locum) are treated as retired.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in section 4; no validation is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The log-linear specification is correct: the 'retirement effect' enters as an additive shift in the log outcome that is constant across GPs within a given year-from-retirement and additively separable from the controls.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Implied by equation (1); the paper justifies the log transformation as making estimates interpretable as percentage differences and as alleviating right-skewness, but does not test the functional form.

formal.as_written: ln(yit) = β1yearfromit + β2ageit + β3patit + β4geoi + β5listsizeit + Tt + εit,

threats_discussed: A cohort effect may be imperfectly separated from the 'retirement effect', especially for late retirees, because few non-retiring GPs are of the same old age.
Non-retiring GPs are on average only 6.4 years younger and a significant share of them may also be nearing retirement, which makes the estimate conservative.
The analysis covers only single-handed practices, who may behave differently from GPs in partnership practices; estimates are likely conservative relative to partnership practices.
The goodwill/selling-price rule gives GPs a financial incentive to maintain revenue in the last three years, which would make the estimates conservative; the authors argue the incentive is weak.
The Charlson Comorbidity Index is an imperfect proxy for GPs' and patients' health status.
The outcome set is limited by register content and cannot capture all clinically relevant behaviour or the quality of care.
The balanced ten-year sample is restrictive and may select GPs.
robustness_checks: Model 2: the same specification augmented with observable GP characteristics (gender, number of children, marital status, previously generated income, health status) - appendix A3.
Heterogeneity analysis splitting retiring GPs by whether they retire before or after the state pension age of 65.
Reducing the analysis period from ten to five years (appendix A4); all results are robust except 'the number of patients joining the list per year'.
Estimating the models without the time-averaged (Mundlak) covariates using OLS with standard errors clustered at GP level (appendix A6).
unresolved_confounders: A cohort effect that is imperfectly separated from the 'retirement effect', which the authors say they cannot exclude as (partly) driving the results, in particular for the late retirees.

estimator.value: Mundlak correlated random effects (random-effects panel regression augmented with GP-level means of the time-varying covariates), with standard errors clustered at GP level

estimation.specification: Model 1, equation (1): the natural log of the outcome regressed on dummies for 10 to 1 years from retirement (reference: GPs not retiring during the analysis period), the GP's age, patient population characteristics, geographical area, list size (omitted when the outcome is list size, join or leave), calendar-year dummies (baseline 2005) and Mundlak GP-level means of all time-varying covariates except the yearfrom and calendar-year dummies.

Mundlak correction terms: GP-level means of all time-varying covariates (except the yearfrom dummies and the calendar year dummies)

ambiguities: The paper describes every estimate as an association (a 'retirement effect' defined as the association between practice style and years from retirement over and above a cohort effect), not as a causal effect; identification.strategy is recorded as selection_on_observables because the design rests on adjusting for observed cohort, patient, geographic and time factors, but 'descriptive' would also be defensible.

baseline_mean and outcome_sd are the non-retiring GPs' mean and standard deviation of the outcome in levels (Table 1, averages at practice level over 2005-2016); the regression outcome is the natural log of that variable, so the two are not in identical units. The paper itself uses the Table 1 non-retiring mean this way when interpreting the home-visit estimates.

Polarity is recorded as higher_is_more for the immediate concept the variable measures (the annual count of patients leaving / joining the list); under a broader 'patient retention' concept the Leave variable would point the other way.

value.as_printed: ln(yit) = β1yearfromit + β2ageit + β3patit + β4geoi + β5listsizeit + Tt + εit,
value.parameter_of_interest: β1 (the vector of coefficients on the yearfrom dummies)
value.normalisation: Reference category for the yearfrom dummies is GPs who are not retiring during the analysis period; calendar-year dummies have baseline 2005; region dummies have baseline The North Denmark Region; the urban indicator has baseline rural; the outcome is in natural logs; listsizeit is omitted when the outcome is list size, join or leave.

value.claimed_domain: Danish single-handed general practice, where GPs are remunerated primarily through fee-for-service and work under contract with the Danish Regions.
boundary_conditions: Policymakers should be careful generalising the findings to settings where GPs' market conditions are markedly different than in Denmark.
The results may not hold when GPs are paid by other payment schemes than fee-for-service.
GPs in partnership practices may behave differently from the single-handed GPs studied; for them the estimated 'retirement effect' would likely be larger (the estimates here are conservative).

baseline_mean and outcome_sd are the non-retiring GPs' mean and standard deviation of the outcome in levels (Table 1, averages at practice level over 2005-2016); the regression outcome is the natural log of that variable, so the two are not in identical units. The coefficient carries no significance star, so sign is recorded as 'null'; the point estimate itself is negative (-0.046).

Polarity is recorded as higher_is_more for the immediate concept the variable measures (the annual count of patients leaving / joining the list); under a broader 'patient retention' concept the Leave variable would point the other way.

evidence.how: The coefficient carries no significance star and Table 2's note defines *p < 0.10, **p < 0.05, ***p < 0.01; the estimate is therefore not statistically distinguishable from zero at the 10% level, which is how the paper reads the absence of a 'retirement effect'.

identification.source_of_variation: Observational contrast between single-handed GPs who retire within 2015-2017, indexed by dummies for the number of years before retirement, and GPs who have not retired by the end of 2017, conditional on GP age (cohort), patient population characteristics, geography, calendar year, list size and Mundlak GP-level means. treatment.label: Being 2 years from retirement (2.yearfrom), i.e. a retiring GP observed 2 years before retirement, relative to GPs who are not retiring during the analysis period

register_source.value: Provider register (GPs' date of retirement; a GP is defined as retired when they no longer appear in the provider register; GPs are identified by their social security number being linked to a provider number)

definition.value: Dummy variable in the vector yearfrom indicating that the retiring GP is 2 years from retirement. The vector covers year 10 to year 1 before retirement; the GP's year of retirement itself is disregarded because the exact retirement date is uncertain. Retiring GPs are those who retire within 2015-2017; the reference category is GPs who are not retiring during the analysis period (not retired by the end of 2017).

timing.value: Calendar year t that falls 2 years before the GP's retirement year (within 2005-2016); the retirement year itself is excluded.

register_source.value: National Health Service register (GPs' provided services and obtained fees)

definition.value: Natural log of the number of home visits the GP provides to patients per year. Because list size is controlled for, the paper interprets the estimate as home visits per enlisted patient.

timing.value: Measured in the same calendar year t as the treatment dummy, i.e. 2 years before retirement; annual totals at practice level.

units.value: log points (coefficient on the natural log of the outcome); the paper states all estimates can be interpreted as %Δy = 100·(e^β - 1)

magnitude.interpretation: part of the ‘16–20 percent’ fewer home visits per patient the paper reports for the last couple of years prior to retirement

estimand.target_population: Single-handed Danish general practices (GPs) observed in a balanced ten-year panel within 2005-2016; the contrast is between GPs who retire within 2015-2017 and GPs who have not retired by the end of 2017.

population.description: 555 single-handed Danish general practices (398 non-retiring GPs and 157 retiring GPs) and their enlisted patients aged 18 and above, observed as a balanced panel over a ten-year period within 2005-2016.
population.ages: Retiring GPs are 57.13 years old on average at baseline and non-retiring GPs 50.71; GPs who retire below the age of 60 are excluded. Patients are aged 18 and above.
subgroups_defined: retiring GPs vs non-retiring GPs
early retirees (retiring before the state pension age of 65) vs late retirees (retiring at 65 or above)
population.selection: Seven exclusion criteria: single-handed practices only; GPs excluded if they change practice or are affiliated to multiple practices during the analysis period; GPs must be active (billing at least one service per year) throughout the period; practices with multiple owners in any year excluded; only GPs retiring above age 60 included; GPs with fewer than 500 patients on their lists excluded; GPs must have a social security number registered in the provider register. identification.source_of_variation: Observational contrast between single-handed GPs who retire within 2015-2017, indexed by dummies for the number of years before retirement, and GPs who have not retired by the end of 2017, conditional on GP age (cohort), patient population characteristics, geography, calendar year, list size and Mundlak GP-level means. population.ages: Retiring GPs are 57.13 years old on average at baseline and non-retiring GPs 50.71; GPs who retire below the age of 60 are excluded. Patients are aged 18 and above.
subgroups_defined: retiring GPs vs non-retiring GPs
early retirees (retiring before the state pension age of 65) vs late retirees (retiring at 65 or above)
population.selection: Seven exclusion criteria: single-handed practices only; GPs excluded if they change practice or are affiliated to multiple practices during the analysis period; GPs must be active (billing at least one service per year) throughout the period; practices with multiple owners in any year excluded; only GPs retiring above age 60 included; GPs with fewer than 500 patients on their lists excluded; GPs must have a social security number registered in the provider register. The panel is balanced over ten years.

identification.source_of_variation: Observational contrast between single-handed GPs who retire within 2015-2017, indexed by dummies for the number of years before retirement, and GPs who have not retired by the end of 2017, conditional on GP age (cohort), patient population characteristics, geography, calendar year, list size and Mundlak GP-level means. No reform, lottery or discontinuity is used; the authors describe the estimate as an association.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the GP's age, their patients' characteristics, geographical area, list size, calendar year and the Mundlak GP-level means of the time-varying covariates, being a given number of years from retirement is unrelated to the remaining (unobserved) determinants of practice style, so the estimated difference is the 'retirement effect' over and above a cohort effect and exogenous factors.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper motivates each control (age for cohort, patient characteristics for demand, calendar year for time trends, geography for access to secondary care) and adds Mundlak correction terms to absorb time-invariant GP and patient characteristics; it does not test the assumption and frames results as associations.

given: Mundlak GP-level means of time-varying covariates

key_assumptions.assumption: The cohort effect is separated from the 'retirement effect' by the control for the GP's own age; the authors concede this separation may be imperfect, especially for the late retirees, because few non-retiring GPs are as old as the late retirees.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No test; the paper states in the discussion that it cannot exclude the possibility that a cohort effect is imperfectly separated from the 'retirement effect' and thereby (partly) drives the results.

implies_edges.from: cohort effect (GP birth cohort not captured by age)
cohort effect (GP birth cohort not captured by age)

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditioning the sample on being a single-handed practice that is active (billing at least one service per year), has at least 500 enlisted patients, has a single owner and is observed in a balanced ten-year panel does not distort the comparison.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper motivates the balanced sample as ensuring stability of practice style outcomes and reports a supplementary analysis with a five-year period (appendix A4), in which all results except 'the number of patients joining the list per year' are robust.

implies_edges.to: sample inclusion (active single-handed practice with >=500 patients, balanced ten-year panel)

key_assumptions.assumption: A GP's retirement is correctly dated by their disappearance from the provider register; because the exact retirement date is uncertain the year of retirement itself is dropped, and GPs who continue consulting after selling their provider number (e.g. as a locum) are treated as retired.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in section 4; no validation is offered.

key_assumptions.assumption: The log-linear specification is correct: the 'retirement effect' enters as an additive shift in the log outcome that is constant across GPs within a given year-from-retirement and additively separable from the controls.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Implied by equation (1); the paper justifies the log transformation as making estimates interpretable as percentage differences and as alleviating right-skewness, but does not test the functional form.

formal.as_written: ln(yit) = β1yearfromit + β2ageit + β3patit + β4geoi + β5listsizeit + Tt + εit,

threats_discussed: A cohort effect may be imperfectly separated from the 'retirement effect', especially for late retirees, because few non-retiring GPs are of the same old age.
Non-retiring GPs are on average only 6.4 years younger and a significant share of them may also be nearing retirement, which makes the estimate conservative.
The analysis covers only single-handed practices, who may behave differently from GPs in partnership practices; estimates are likely conservative relative to partnership practices.
The goodwill/selling-price rule gives GPs a financial incentive to maintain revenue in the last three years, which would make the estimates conservative; the authors argue the incentive is weak.
The Charlson Comorbidity Index is an imperfect proxy for GPs' and patients' health status.
The outcome set is limited by register content and cannot capture all clinically relevant behaviour or the quality of care.
The balanced ten-year sample is restrictive and may select GPs.
robustness_checks: Model 2: the same specification augmented with observable GP characteristics (gender, number of children, marital status, previously generated income, health status) - appendix A3.
Heterogeneity analysis splitting retiring GPs by whether they retire before or after the state pension age of 65.
Reducing the analysis period from ten to five years (appendix A4); all results are robust except 'the number of patients joining the list per year'.
Estimating the models without the time-averaged (Mundlak) covariates using OLS with standard errors clustered at GP level (appendix A6).
unresolved_confounders: A cohort effect that is imperfectly separated from the 'retirement effect', which the authors say they cannot exclude as (partly) driving the results, in particular for the late retirees.

estimator.value: Mundlak correlated random effects (random-effects panel regression augmented with GP-level means of the time-varying covariates), with standard errors clustered at GP level

ambiguities: The paper describes every estimate as an association (a 'retirement effect' defined as the association between practice style and years from retirement over and above a cohort effect), not as a causal effect; identification.strategy is recorded as selection_on_observables because the design rests on adjusting for observed cohort, patient, geographic and time factors, but 'descriptive' would also be defensible.

baseline_mean and outcome_sd are the non-retiring GPs' mean and standard deviation of the outcome in levels (Table 1, averages at practice level over 2005-2016); the regression outcome is the natural log of that variable, so the two are not in identical units. The paper itself uses the Table 1 non-retiring mean this way when interpreting the home-visit estimates.

List size is included as a control so that the estimate can be read 'per enlisted patient'; because list size itself responds to approaching retirement in this paper, it is recorded in adjustment_set with role 'mediator' rather than 'confounder'.

value.as_printed: ln(yit) = β1yearfromit + β2ageit + β3patit + β4geoi + β5listsizeit + Tt + εit,
value.parameter_of_interest: β1 (the vector of coefficients on the yearfrom dummies)
value.normalisation: Reference category for the yearfrom dummies is GPs who are not retiring during the analysis period; calendar-year dummies have baseline 2005; region dummies have baseline The North Denmark Region; the urban indicator has baseline rural; the outcome is in natural logs; listsizeit is omitted when the outcome is list size, join or leave.

value.claimed_domain: Danish single-handed general practice, where GPs are remunerated primarily through fee-for-service and work under contract with the Danish Regions.
boundary_conditions: Policymakers should be careful generalising the findings to settings where GPs' market conditions are markedly different than in Denmark.
The results may not hold when GPs are paid by other payment schemes than fee-for-service.
GPs in partnership practices may behave differently from the single-handed GPs studied; for them the estimated 'retirement effect' would likely be larger (the estimates here are conservative).

falsification.condition: The paper states that a 'retirement effect' exists if the estimates of the yearfrom coefficients are statistically significantly different from zero; statistically insignificant estimates are read as the absence of a 'retirement effect'.

anchor_quote.text: ‘The retirement effect’ on all practice style outcomes by year from retirement (model 1).

claims.statement: Conditional on GP age, patient characteristics, geography, calendar year and list size, single-handed Danish GPs observed 6 years before retirement have a higher number of referrals to private practice specialists per enlisted patient (in logs) than GPs who are not retiring during the analysis period.

treatment.label: Being 6 years from retirement (6.yearfrom), i.e. a retiring GP observed 6 years before retirement, relative to GPs who are not retiring during the analysis period

register_source.value: Provider register (GPs' date of retirement; a GP is defined as retired when they no longer appear in the provider register; GPs are identified by their social security number being linked to a provider number)

definition.value: Dummy variable in the vector yearfrom indicating that the retiring GP is 6 years from retirement. The vector covers year 10 to year 1 before retirement; the GP's year of retirement itself is disregarded because the exact retirement date is uncertain. Retiring GPs are those who retire within 2015-2017; the reference category is GPs who are not retiring during the analysis period (not retired by the end of 2017).

timing.value: Calendar year t that falls 6 years before the GP's retirement year (within 2005-2016); the retirement year itself is excluded.

register_source.value: National Health Service register (referrals made to private practice specialists)

definition.value: Natural log of the number of referrals to private practising secondary care specialists per year; the number of referrals is quantified using the separate fee the specialist receives for a consultation related to a new referral. Because list size is controlled for, the paper interprets the estimate as referrals per enlisted patient.

timing.value: Measured in the same calendar year t as the treatment dummy, i.e. 6 years before retirement; annual totals at practice level.

units.value: log points (coefficient on the natural log of the outcome); the paper states all estimates can be interpreted as %Δy = 100·(e^β - 1)

magnitude.interpretation: part of the ‘6–9 percent’ more patients referred to private practice specialists that the paper reports across its ten-year observation period

baseline_mean and outcome_sd are the non-retiring GPs' mean and standard deviation of the outcome in levels (Table 1, averages at practice level over 2005-2016); the regression outcome is the natural log of that variable, so the two are not in identical units. The paper itself uses the Table 1 non-retiring mean this way when interpreting the home-visit estimates.

List size is included as a control so that the estimate can be read 'per enlisted patient'; because list size itself responds to approaching retirement in this paper, it is recorded in adjustment_set with role 'mediator' rather than 'confounder'.

links.pointer_quote: We also find that retirement is associated with other dimensions of GPs’ practice style, e.g. their provision of home visits, prescribing, and referral rates.

claims.statement: Conditional on GP age, patient characteristics, geography, calendar year and list size, single-handed Danish GPs observed 1 year before retirement have a higher number of referrals to private practice specialists per enlisted patient (in logs) than GPs who are not retiring during the analysis period.

treatment.label: Being 1 year from retirement (1.yearfrom), i.e. a retiring GP observed 1 year before retirement, relative to GPs who are not retiring during the analysis period

register_source.value: Provider register (GPs' date of retirement; a GP is defined as retired when they no longer appear in the provider register; GPs are identified by their social security number being linked to a provider number)

definition.value: Dummy variable in the vector yearfrom indicating that the retiring GP is 1 year from retirement. The vector covers year 10 to year 1 before retirement; the GP's year of retirement itself is disregarded because the exact retirement date is uncertain. Retiring GPs are those who retire within 2015-2017; the reference category is GPs who are not retiring during the analysis period (not retired by the end of 2017).

timing.value: Calendar year t that falls 1 year before the GP's retirement year (within 2005-2016); the retirement year itself is excluded.

register_source.value: National Health Service register (referrals made to private practice specialists)

definition.value: Natural log of the number of referrals to private practising secondary care specialists per year; the number of referrals is quantified using the separate fee the specialist receives for a consultation related to a new referral. Because list size is controlled for, the paper interprets the estimate as referrals per enlisted patient.

timing.value: Measured in the same calendar year t as the treatment dummy, i.e. 1 year before retirement; annual totals at practice level.

units.value: log points (coefficient on the natural log of the outcome); the paper states all estimates can be interpreted as %Δy = 100·(e^β - 1)

magnitude.interpretation: part of the ‘6–9 percent’ more patients referred to private practice specialists that the paper reports across its ten-year observation period

estimand.target_population: Single-handed Danish general practices (GPs) observed in a balanced ten-year panel within 2005-2016; the contrast is between GPs who retire within 2015-2017 and GPs who have not retired by the end of 2017.

population.description: 555 single-handed Danish general practices (398 non-retiring GPs and 157 retiring GPs) and their enlisted patients aged 18 and above, observed as a balanced panel over a ten-year period within 2005-2016.
population.ages: Retiring GPs are 57.13 years old on average at baseline and non-retiring GPs 50.71; GPs who retire below the age of 60 are excluded. Patients are aged 18 and above.
subgroups_defined: retiring GPs vs non-retiring GPs
early retirees (retiring before the state pension age of 65) vs late retirees (retiring at 65 or above)
population.selection: Seven exclusion criteria: single-handed practices only; GPs excluded if they change practice or are affiliated to multiple practices during the analysis period; GPs must be active (billing at least one service per year) throughout the period; practices with multiple owners in any year excluded; only GPs retiring above age 60 included; GPs with fewer than 500 patients on their lists excluded; GPs must have a social security number registered in the provider register. The panel is balanced over ten years.

identification.source_of_variation: Observational contrast between single-handed GPs who retire within 2015-2017, indexed by dummies for the number of years before retirement, and GPs who have not retired by the end of 2017, conditional on GP age (cohort), patient population characteristics, geography, calendar year, list size and Mundlak GP-level means. No reform, lottery or discontinuity is used; the authors describe the estimate as an association.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the GP's age, their patients' characteristics, geographical area, list size, calendar year and the Mundlak GP-level means of the time-varying covariates, being a given number of years from retirement is unrelated to the remaining (unobserved) determinants of practice style, so the estimated difference is the 'retirement effect' over and above a cohort effect and exogenous factors.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper motivates each control (age for cohort, patient characteristics for demand, calendar year for time trends, geography for access to secondary care) and adds Mundlak correction terms to absorb time-invariant GP and patient characteristics; it does not test the assumption and frames results as associations.
